fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Hemorrhage By reading this page you agree to ACOG's Terms and Conditions. Read terms ABSTRACT: Maternal hemorrhage, defined as a cumulative blood loss of greater than or equal to 1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after the birth process, remains the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide 1. Additional important secondary sequelae from hemorrhage exist and include adult respiratory distress syndrome, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute renal failure, loss of fertility, and pituitary necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). Hemorrhage that leads to blood transfusion is the leading cause of severe maternal morbidity in the United States closely followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation 2. In the United States, the rate of postpartum hemorrhage increased 26% between 1994 and 2006 primarily because of increased rates of atony 3. In contrast, maternal mortality from postpartum obstetric hemorrhage has decreased since the late 1980s and accounted for slightly more than 10% of maternal mortalities (approximately 1.7 deaths per 100,000 live births) in 2009 2 4. This observed decrease in mortality is associated with increasing rates of transfusion and peripartum hysterectomy 2 3 4. The purpose of this Practice Bulletin is to discuss the risk factors for postpartum hemorrhage as well as its evaluation, prevention, and management. In addition, this document will encourage obstetrician–gynecologists and other obstetric care providers to play key roles in implementing standardized bundles of care (eg, policies, guidelines, and algorithms) for the management of postpartum hemorrhage. fetched_contents.text: Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage Abstract Postpartum haemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. However, postpartum haemorrhage-related deaths are potentially preventable with timely diagnosis and management. The present review addresses the management of postpartum haemorrhage algorithm that includes the use of uterotonics, non-surgical (balloon tamponade) or surgical (sutures, artery ligations, and/or hysterectomy) techniques, and/or endovascular radiologic interventions, antifibrinolytic (tranexamic acid), and procoagulant (fibrinogen concentrate) drugs based on the international and national guidelines updated with recent evidences. Keywords: Algorithm, guideline, management, obstetrics, postpartum haemorrhage ---------------------------------------- Main Points * Postpartum hemorrhage remains a clinically significant cause of maternal complications and death worldwide. * To decrease maternal mortality, using a postpartum hemorrhage algorithm with trigger and target values is recommended. * Management should include surgical/nonsurgical techniques/maneuvers along with evidence based use of massive transfusion protocol modified according to the facility needs/resources including hemostatic and/or pro-coagulant agents under the guidance of standard and/or point of care tests by multidisciplinary approach. Introduction The aim of this present review is to address the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) based on the international and national guidelines updated with recent evidence. Definition According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecolgists, PPH is defined as a cumulative blood loss greater than or equal to 1000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolaemia within 24 hours after the birth process (includes intrapartum loss) regardless of route of delivery.1 The PPH is categorised as either primary or secondary; primary occurs in the first 24 hours after delivery (early PPH) and secondary PPH occurs 24 hours to 12 weeks after delivery (late or delayed PPH).2 According to global, regional, and national levels of maternal mortality rate (MMR) between 1990 and 2013, a systematic analysis of the global burden of disease study showed that 292 982 (95% UI: 261 017-327 792) maternal deaths occurred in 2013, compared with 376 034 (343 483-407 574) in 1990. Globally, the biggest absolute reduction was observed in death rates due to maternal haemorrhage from 71 295 (95% UI: 64 562-78 329) in 1990 to 44 190 (38 273-50 819) in 2013.3 The MMR has been most commonly resulted from PPH in Turkey with a rate of 13.1 in 100 000 live births in 2019.4 Therefore, vigilance and awareness about risk factors are very important before delivery. Risk Factors According to the multidisciplinary consensus statement, the prediction of PPH is difficult and there is no single risk factor except abnormal placentation. Despite number of contributing risk factors (multiple pregnancies, history of PPH, pregnancy-induced hypertension, chorioamnionitis, episiotomy, pre-labour caesarean section, macrosomia, and operative vaginal delivery), PPH can develop unpredictably without any risk factor.2 Therefore, any maternal unit should be prepared to manage PPH with physicians in charge of maternal care. Main causes of PPH are represented by 4Ts (tone 70%, tissue 20%, trauma 10%, and thrombin <1%) which should be checked during management, and treatment should be directed accordingly. Uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH, and others include genital tract trauma, uterine rupture, retained placental tissue, and maternal coagulation disorders.2 General Principles of Postpartum Haemorrhage Management Management of PPH necessitates a coordinated multidisciplinary approach which involves good communication including an obstetrician–perinatologist, anaesthesiologist, haematologist–blood bank and interventional radiologist, for accurate assessment of blood loss, monitoring of maternal signs and symptoms, fluid, blood and blood product replacement, and arrest of the source of the haemorrhage.5 Assessment of Blood Loss Measuring blood loss as accurately as possible is essential for identifying the severity of haemorrhage and assessing patient’s response to haemorrhage. According to a pictorial reference guide to aid visual estimation of blood loss, the amount of blood estimations are soiled sanitary towel (30 mL), soaked sanitary towel (100 mL), small soaked swab 10 × 10 (60 mL), large soaked swab 45 × 45 (350 mL), and full kidney dish (500 mL). Additionally, blood in aspiratory tubes (includes amnion fluid as well) under buttocks drapes and surgery site (blood pooling) needs to be considered.6 However, in visual estimations, rate of misdiagnosis is around 35%-50%. Therefore, instead of estimated blood loss (EBL), since it is always very difficult as well as late, quantitative measurement is recommended. Immediate interventions and escalation protocol

First-line uterotonic agents and dosing
The evidence supports a stepped approach starting with uterotonic drugs. ACOG defines postpartum hemorrhage as cumulative blood loss ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth, and recommends standardized bundles of care for management [N1-F1]. The PPH management review also emphasizes uterotonics such as oxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost, or misoprostol, along with non-surgical/surgical techniques, antifibrinolytic drugs, and procoagulant agents as part of the management algorithm [N2-F2]. Specifically, the evidence-based review notes that oxytocin is a central agent, while the “Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage” source states that prophylactic Syntocinon infusion may be used at 40 units of Syntocinon in 500 mL sodium chloride at 125 mL/hour [N2-R5]. This is consistent with the idea of a first-line uterotonic protocol rather than a single drug.

When to escalate to IV fluids, blood products, and surgical intervention
The evidence indicates escalation should occur early if hemorrhage persists or worsens. The PPH management review explicitly states that management should be directed by the 4Ts—tone, tissue, trauma, thrombin—and that surgical/nonsurgical techniques, along with massive transfusion protocols, are indicated depending on facility resources and patient response [N2-F2]. It also notes that the use of a trigger and target value algorithm is recommended to decrease maternal mortality [N2-F2]. The evidence further supports that massive transfusion is part of the algorithm when bleeding is severe and ongoing [N2-F2]. The WHO-quality-of-care standards emphasize evidence-based interventions during critical periods of care, including labor and delivery management, which supports the need for timely escalation [N3-R4]. In practice, persistent hemorrhage after uterotonic administration and uterine massage should prompt reassessment and escalation, including IV fluids, blood products, and surgical intervention such as balloon tamponade, compression sutures, artery ligation, or hysterectomy [N2-F2].

How to document interventions and time points
Documentation should be chronological and explicit. The labor and delivery evidence base emphasizes evidence-based guidance for management decisions during labor and delivery [N3-R3], while WHO standards stress prioritized, evidence-based interventions during critical periods of care [N3-R4]. The evidence also supports recording events and interventions in order, including time points, because the management of PPH requires coordinated communication among obstetricians, anaesthesiologists, haematologists, blood bank staff, and interventional radiologists [N2-F2]. The “OBRx — Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) Management Algorithm” excerpt notes that if active hemorrhage occurs, reassessment should happen every few minutes and escalation should be early [N4-R3]. This implies that documentation should capture time of onset, interventions, dosing, response, and any changes in status. The labor documentation standards also imply that notes should include patient response and outcome, as they are part of the overall labor and delivery record structure [N3-R5]. For continuity and audit, the note should include all interventions, time points, and the patient’s response, as the PPH management review emphasizes coordinated assessment, monitoring, fluid/blood replacement, and arrest of the source of hemorrhage [N2-F2].

Bottom line
The immediate intervention pathway is: uterotonic drugs first, with oxytocin and prophylactic Syntocinon infusion as examples [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Escalation is indicated when bleeding persists, signs of hypovolemia develop, or the patient deteriorates, and should include IV fluids, blood products, and surgical/surgical-adjacent interventions [N2-F2]. Documentation should be chronological, capturing interventions, time points, and patient response, with enough detail to support continuity and audit [N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-R3].

Evidence-based context for decision-making and risk communication

Outcomes associated with 1800 mL EBL and related complications
The evidence clearly associates large blood loss with significant complications. ACOG states that maternal hemorrhage defined as cumulative blood loss ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia remains the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide [N1-F1]. The PPH management review similarly describes PPH as a clinically significant cause of maternal complications and death, and notes that maternal deaths from PPH decreased from 71,295 in 1990 to 44,190 in 2013 [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that PPH-related deaths are potentially preventable with timely diagnosis and management [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence on outcomes after PPH includes the need for blood transfusion, hemorrhagic shock, hysterectomy, and other complications, which the Maternal Outcomes of Postpartum Hemorrhage after Vaginal Delivery study examined [N5-R3]. The WHO evidence also links PPH to maternal mortality and morbidity, noting that it causes around 70,000 deaths each year and is the leading cause of maternal mortality [N5-R4]. These outcomes strongly support that 1800 mL EBL is not merely a blood-loss threshold but a clinically meaningful point that warrants urgent action.

Maternal mortality and morbidity risk
The evidence consistently highlights maternal mortality and morbidity risk. ACOG states that hemorrhage that leads to blood transfusion is the leading cause of severe maternal morbidity in the United States, closely followed by disseminated intravascular coagulation [N1-F1]. The PPH review notes that maternal mortality from postpartum obstetric hemorrhage has decreased since the late 1980s but that PPH remains a major cause of maternal death [N2-F2]. The WHO evidence states that PPH is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide and causes around 70,000 deaths each year [N5-R4]. The AHA strategies for improving outcomes note that PPH occurs in 3% to 5% of all deliveries and is responsible for 14.1% of maternal deaths in the United States [N5-R5]. These data together show that 1800 mL EBL is associated with a substantial risk of death and severe morbidity, making it a critical threshold for escalation.

How evidence supports escalation thresholds and treatment choices
The evidence supports escalation thresholds by showing that PPH is best managed with a trigger-and-target-value algorithm, coordinated multidisciplinary care, and early intervention [N2-F2]. The same review supports the use of uterotonic drugs, non-surgical/surgical techniques, antifibrinolytic drugs, and procoagulant agents depending on the situation [N2-F2]. ACOG emphasizes standardized bundles of care, policies, guidelines, and algorithms for management [N1-F1]. The WHO-quality-of-care standards also support evidence-based interventions during critical periods of care, reinforcing the need for timely escalation [N3-R4]. The “OBRx” management algorithm excerpt states that if active hemorrhage occurs, reassessment should be every few minutes and escalation should be early [N4-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports using EBL ≥1,000 mL or hypovolemic signs as a trigger for escalation and using a stepwise treatment pathway that includes uterotonics, IV fluids, blood products, and surgical intervention when needed [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3].

Clinical picture and severity determination

What constitutes postpartum hemorrhage and how 1800 mL EBL is classified
The evidence defines postpartum hemorrhage as cumulative blood loss ≥1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after birth [N1-F1]. The PPH management review states that PPH is defined as a cumulative blood loss greater than or equal to 1,000 mL or blood loss accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours after the birth process, and that PPH is categorized as either primary or secondary, with primary occurring in the first 24 hours after delivery [N2-F2]. The WHO evidence also supports the traditional definition of primary PPH as loss of 500 mL or more of blood from the genital tract within 24 hours after birth, while the ACOG abstract states that the traditional definition is blood loss of more than 500 mL after a vaginal delivery or more than 1,000 mL after a cesarean delivery [N1-R5][N5-R1]. Therefore, 1800 mL EBL is clearly beyond the traditional threshold and represents severe postpartum hemorrhage, not just a borderline case.

Signs and symptoms that support hemorrhage severity beyond blood loss
The evidence explicitly states that signs or symptoms of hypovolemia are part of the definition of postpartum hemorrhage [N1-F1]. The PPH management review also emphasizes that management should be directed by the 4Ts—tone, tissue, trauma, thrombin—and that uterine atony is the most common cause of PPH, with other causes including genital tract trauma, uterine rupture, retained placental tissue, and maternal coagulation disorders [N2-F2]. The ACOG document notes that maternal hemorrhage can lead to adult respiratory distress syndrome, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute renal failure, loss of fertility, and Sheehan syndrome [N1-F1]. These symptoms and sequelae are important because they indicate that hemorrhage severity is not merely measured by blood loss alone but also by the patient’s clinical response. In other words, even if EBL is not yet 1800 mL, signs of hypovolemia, shock, or coagulopathy strongly support escalation [N1-F1][N2-F2].

When hemorrhage becomes life-threatening and requires escalation
The evidence supports escalation when hemorrhage is persistent, signs of hypovolemia develop, or the patient’s condition deteriorates. ACOG states that maternal hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide and that timely diagnosis and management are required to prevent death [N1-F1]. The PPH management review recommends using a trigger and target value algorithm to decrease maternal mortality and emphasizes a coordinated multidisciplinary approach, including fluid and blood replacement and arrest of the source of hemorrhage [N2-F2]. The “OBRx” management algorithm excerpt states that if active hemorrhage occurs, reassessment should be every few minutes and escalation should be early [N4-R3]. This directly supports the idea that hemorrhage becomes life-threatening when it persists despite initial interventions and when early escalation is needed to prevent deterioration. In practice, the evidence supports escalating to IV fluids, blood products, and surgical intervention when the patient shows signs of hypovolemia, ongoing hemorrhage, or impending shock [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R3].

The evidence supports chronological documentation of events and interventions. WHO standards for the quality of maternal and newborn care emphasize evidence-based interventions during critical periods of care [N3-R4]. The “OBRx” management algorithm excerpt notes that if active hemorrhage occurs, reassessment should be every few minutes and escalation should be early [N4-R3], which supports documenting time points and interventions in order. How to capture patient response and outcome
The evidence supports documenting patient response and outcome because the management of PPH requires coordinated assessment, monitoring, fluid and blood replacement, and arrest of the source of hemorrhage [N2-F2]. ACOG states that maternal hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide and that timely diagnosis and management are essential [N1-F1]. The PPH management review also notes that maternal deaths from PPH have decreased since the late 1980s and that PPH remains a major cause of maternal death [N2-F2]. These findings imply that outcome documentation should include vital signs, response to interventions, whether hemorrhage has stopped or continued, and any complications such as shock, transfusion needs, or hysterectomy [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also supports capturing signs of hypovolemia, because those are part of the definition of hemorrhage severity [N1-F1]. Therefore, the note should record not only what was done but also how the patient responded to each intervention.

What should be included in the final note for continuity and audit
The final note should include enough detail to support continuity and audit. WHO standards stress prioritized, evidence-based interventions during critical periods of care [N3-R4]. The evidence-based labor and delivery management source likewise emphasizes evidence-based guidance for management decisions [N3-R3]. The PPH management review emphasizes coordinated communication among obstetricians, anaesthesiologists, haematologists, blood bank staff, and interventional radiologists [N2-F2]. This means the final note should include the patient’s identity, time of birth, estimated blood loss, interventions given, dosing, time of administration, patient response, any transfusions, surgical procedures, and the outcome. The note should also capture any signs of deterioration or escalation, because the evidence supports early reassessment and escalation when active hemorrhage occurs [N4-R3]. For audit purposes, it should be clear what was done, when, and why, so that another provider can understand the clinical pathway and decision-making [N2-F2][N3-R4].
